items.title: Many drugs work by binding to a specific target in the body and blocking or changing what it does. An important first st
items.content:
Many drugs work by binding to a specific target in the body and blocking or changing what it does. An important first step in the drug development process is designing a molecule that can bind tightly to its target. Traditionally, that's meant weeks or months of expert work per target, sifting through a large number of candidates to identify the few that work.

We wanted to test if Claude could successfully design novel protein binders from scratch (also called de novo design). With a protein design prompt written by a human expert, Claude autonomously designed protein binders against 14 out of 15 targets.

We then worked with Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, who independently built and tested the proteins Claude designed.

items.title: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to
items.content:
1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation.

First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice.  I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world.  Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.  I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of.  But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.  A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice.  At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.

This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully.  We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.  California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that).  More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers.  Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up.  This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights!

Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws).  Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers).  By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring.

BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”.  The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure.  I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity.  This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.

items.title: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI.  I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative.  In fact
items.content:
2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI.  I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative.  In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks).  In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better.  The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!).  And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process.  I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him.

I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks.  I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust.  I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over.  The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it.  I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive.  The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*.  I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world.  That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing.

We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months.  When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that.  But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them.  Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

items.title: Seeing a hype wave around GEN-1.5, and rightfully so. Lots of respect to Pete & Andy for executing so well. The secret i
items.content:
Seeing a hype wave around GEN-1.5, and rightfully so. Lots of respect to Pete & Andy for executing so well. The secret is in the naturally repetitive motions in human-collected data. There're 2 main sources for such repetitions: 

(1) Symmetric patterns. Sorting, tidying, and assembling almost never finish in one motion. Open any assembly manual from IKEA, and you find most objects symmetrical. You drive one bolt, then its twin, then the next pair. Every {bolt A, bolt B} pair is a natural continuation in context, and the second instance is a free training signal that imitates the first ("prompt").

(2) Recovery. Humans drop things all the time, but we pick them up so fast, we don’t even notice. That reflex to fix is half of our physical competence. The key insight is to keep the failed first half instead of trimming it away. If the model consumes the full arc, fumble, catch, continue, then recovery shows up organically at test time. It's funny that in-context improvement results from *NOT* over-sanitizing your data.

The other critical ingredient is UMI. I've been saying for a while that teleop will not last, and GEN-1.5 is driving the final nail in the coffin. UMI is essentially a human wearing the robot gripper to collect data directly (human → data). Teleop inserts a layer of separation: human → VR/skeletal device → robot → data, which bleeds out all the human "physical intuition". The subtle sleight of hand we perform constantly with objects, the micro-adjustments, the feel of a part snapping into place, is nearly impossible to capture when you can't feel the environment directly.

Once you have enough data, many behaviors can actually be zero-shot. For example, you don't even need finetuning to pick up a novel object. The model "just knows" what to do given a similar scene in the training distribution. Whether in-context learning truly works or not also depends on how far away the test is from training. Currently, the demos are still a bit too simple to conclude.

I'm cautiously optimistic. Still, it's a great day in robotics.

BOOTSTRAPPED VS VENTURE BACKED STARTUPS

If you run a bootstrapped business using VC strategies, you will lose. They are
items.content:
BOOTSTRAPPED VS VENTURE BACKED STARTUPS

If you run a bootstrapped business using VC strategies, you will lose. They are different games with different rules.

I REALLY felt how different while listening to Travis Kalanick on David Senra.

Travis subsidized rides to buy the market, ate massive losses on purpose to spin up the network effects, and went from a $6B to a $17.5B valuation in 2 months to turn money into a weapon. It's a masterclass.

And if you're bootstrapped, most of the movse he describes belongs to a different sport.

I've built and sold VC-backed startups (one to WeWork, the most VC thing that ever existed lol), and now I'm building a bootstrapped holdco, so I've felt both.

Underpricing to zero is genius in VC and suicide bootstrapped. 

Taking a dividend is smart bootstrapped and crazy in VC. Every strategy only makes sense inside the game you're actually playing.

Same words, growth, win, competition, mean opposite things depending on which game you're in.

And there is no right game or wrong game. 

It's a really personal thing. Some people watch Travis talk about turning money into a weapon and going to war for a market, and they get fired up, that's their game, and they should go raise and swing for the $10B outcome. 

Some people watch the same clip and think that sounds like a nightmare, they'd rather own the whole thing, get paid every month, and answer to nobody. 

I think both are great. You just have to know which one you are.

They're just different lives.

2) If I have $400/mo to spare, I’d use both Claude Code and Codex 

2) If I have $200/mo, I’d use the Codex 20x plan 

3) If I have $100/mo and I view tiny blockers as fun things to push past, I’d use the Codex 5x plan 

4) If I have $100/mo and I view tiny blockers as utter hell, I’d use Claude Cowork 

4) If I have $20/mo, I’d use Codex and ChatGPT and just focus on scheduled tasks

items.title: Show HN: Huzzah – a novel approach to coding with AI
items.content:
Show HN: Huzzah – a novel approach to coding with AI Hello everyone. I've been working on this experimental editor called Huzzah.

I've been working almost exclusively with coding agents since January of this year, and over the past few months I began to feel utterly exhausted by them. They're great, but I'm finding it more and more tedious to write full sentences for every change I want. Not only that, but it seems there's a complexity limit for codebases - beyond a certain point the agent begins confusing itself.

I'd like to go back to writing code, but I don't want to go all the way back to fully manual coding. So I've come up with this interaction paradigm where you:

  1. write pseudocode in whatever way makes the most sense to you
  2. on save, the editor synchronizes your work to real source code
  3. the pseudocode is persisted alongside the generated code, making your prompt effectively a stored record of intent.
It may not work for every use case, but in my initial playthroughs I've found it very enjoyable.

Right now it's just a proof of concept - installation instructions are here in the readme: https://github.com/danielvaughn/hz

You can also watch a video of it in action here: https://x.com/danielvaughn/status/2090456808431165715

Cheers!

items.content:
Show HN: Check if any of the $656M in unclaimed royalties at The MLC is yours Hi HN, I built this. Quick background on why it exists:

When music is streamed on digital streaming platforms (think Spotify, Apple Music, Pandora), there are two separate royalty streams: one for the recording, paid through your distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, CDBaby), and one for the underlying work (generally known as publishing). The work side's mechanical royalties are collected by The MLC, a nonprofit that was created by the 2018 Music Modernization Act (MMA). If you haven't registered your songs with The MLC, there are issues with your metadata, or about half a dozen other reasons, that money will never reach you, it just collects in a big pile we call the "black box".

That pile is big. The MLC's own dashboard currently shows over $656M is held (themlc.com/blanket-royalties), and the biggest problem is the MMA dictates that The MLC cannot hold that money indefinitely. At some point, by law, The MLC must distribute this big pile of cash, and since they don't know who it's supposed to go to, they pay it out through a process called "market share" (themlc.com/marketshare). Market share means they pay it out, pro-rata, to the artists, songwriters and publishers that are in the system, which in practice means the largest publishers collect most of the leftovers.

This is slated to begin in January 2027 and will pay portions of the pool out monthly (themlc.com/unclaimed-accrued-royalties), as of this morning, the next 12 months of market share sums up to $76.61M, starting with $6.41M in January.

Full disclosure: I run Doubly, which is an independent publishing administrator, so I have a commercial interest in this space. That being said, we're a team of two people and we don't have the bandwidth to directly assist the hundreds of thousands of artists and songwriters who are going to start losing this money in January 2027.

That's why I built this self-service tool, no signup, no email, no paywall, the reports are completely actionable without needing anything from us.

The tool: paste a Spotify artist link (or search for a Spotify artist by name). It pulls every release on that profile, checks each recording against The MLC's public bulk data, and tells you per-song whether it's fully claimed, partially claimed, registered but unmatched, or missing entirely. It then provides a link to the exact MLC tool that fixes each case. It also estimates the dollars stuck, as a rough range.

Even if you're not an artist yourself, you probably know someone who is a musician, please share it with them.

Thanks for your time and I'm happy to answer any questions about the industry as a whole, The MLC, the tech, anything really.

The best way to make an AI agent faster is a permission list.

Here is why it works: you delegate to an agent the same way you do to an employee: safe tasks, permissioned tasks, blocked tasks. Sort each task into one of the three groups, and you always know how much room the agent has. 

A clear breakdown of each bucket:

1) Safe actions:
- Read files and inspect the code base.
- Propose plans and run local tests.
- Edit a small feature branch, update the docs, open a draft pull request.

2) Ask-first actions:
- Install dependencies.
- Change a database migration or touch authentication.
- Change the payment logic.
- Delete files.

3) Human-owned actions: 
- Production deploys.
- Customer data decisions.
- Billing decisions.
- Security-sensitive changes.

Then set the permission mode in Claude Desktop to match. Start with strict limits. 

Use plan mode for the large changes. Use manual review while you learn the system. 

Give the agent more access as your repo notes, your review checklist, and your task scopes get stronger. 

So start your permission list today and sort each task accordingly

When TIME visited Unitree’s Hangzhou headquarters, their founder Wang Xingxing wouldn’t get in or even turn it on, because “It might not be safe,” he said.

That’s a striking thing to hear from the biggest humanoid maker in the world, a company shipping over 5,500 units last year.

It just filed for a $6B IPO, and has pushed its flagship G1 down to $13,500 by building its own actuators, the motors that make up most of a humanoid’s cost.

But the numbers underneath tell a stranger story. Only 9% of its humanoid sales go to real industrial work.

74% go to universities and developers, meaning the industry is largely selling robots to people trying to build better robots.

Hardware is racing ahead. The software that makes these machines genuinely useful is still the hard part.

items.content:
this is one of the most critical pieces we’ve shipped to date, crossing nearly 1,000 npm downloads in a single day. i know package manager stats might not mean much if you don't write code, but think of it like building a skyscraper. everyone wants to see the glass penthouse and the flashy skyline view, but none of that exists without pouring the concrete foundation and laying the steel framework first. 

the market always demands flashy promises and immediate "utility," but the data proves developers are actively using our framework. i want to share where we are actually heading and why these "invisible" building blocks we are shipping today are the only way to get there.

ar is not the endgame. we are not just placing 3d models into your physical space through a lens; we are preparing to bring them into absolute reality. today, they live as spatial entities on https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF. tomorrow, they manifest physically through 3d printing. eventually, they become the cognitive and economic software layer for real-world robotics.

but ideas are cheap, and the physical world is unforgiving. before an agent can safely inhabit a robotic chassis, it needs a nervous system, a verifiable onchain passport, and a bank account. you cannot skip the infrastructure. that is why we are obsessively laying down the building blocks today with onchain identity standards, the mcp rails, the x402 economy so that when the hardware catches up, the os is already alive.

today you can type a sentence and a fully embodied 3d ai agent appears in your room. drop it at a real-world gps coordinate on https://t.co/xtZ0kK4bTU, and it stays exactly where you left it. strangers who walk past your spot will meet it. and now, those agents have wallets and the ability to transact right there on the pavement. of everything we've shipped, this is the one i've been waiting to show you.
if you've been with us a while, you've watched a lot of pieces land. free text-to-3d in the browser. avatars that rig and walk on their own. agents with wallets. paid tools over x402. a chatgpt app. worlds you can speak into existence. and now agents pinned to real gps coordinates, standing on your street, at your shop door, on your desk.

forge is the body. type a sentence, and a being exists that took a specialist weeks to make two years ago. irl is the place. pin it to the world and it stays, and people who walk past your spot meet it. x402 is how it earns. agents on https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF already pay each other in stablecoins for real work, and that economy grows whether anyone is watching or not.

we just made it possible to watch.

i. the body: breaking the chatbox
the ai chatbox is a ghost. we have spent the last three years talking to floating text windows. but human beings are spatial creatures. we are built to interact with physical entities that have presence, emotion, and reaction.

text and image to 3d model is by far the most advanced tool the crypto and ai sectors have seen to date. it's the exact paradigm shift that helped tripo ai raise $200m at a $1b valuation. at https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF, we are bringing that exact level of frictionless creation directly into the open web, entirely open-source.

when you use our forge, you are interacting with the bleeding edge of inference. powered by our partnership with nvidia inception and leveraging nvidia nim, we can take a text prompt, a selfie, or a rough sketch, and output a rig-ready, 200k-poly pbr textured 3d model in under a minute.

but a mesh is just a shell. to make it a body, we built a four-layer webgl 2.0 rendering engine that runs entirely in the browser. no plugins. no downloads.

the brain: we route through ibm watsonx, granite, openai, and claude to give the agent flawless, low-latency reasoning.

the empathy layer: agents don’t have hard-coded "happy" or "sad" animations. we built a continuous emotion blend system. morph target weights update every single frame based on the live sentiment of the conversation.

the voice: real-time arkit-52 lip-sync and voice cloning.

when you embed our <agent-3d> web component on your site, you are dropping in a fully embodied entity that can physically read your dom, cover its eyes when a user types a password, and facepalm when a form submission fails.

ii. the place: the living spatial web
agents need a world to inhabit.

imagine placing a 3d ai agent anywhere in the world and doing irl business through you. you can't see it normally, but if you have https://t.co/8Xiy9XFb7s or https://t.co/rIkpE1vmYf open with your phone camera or smart glasses, you can send crypto or interact with the ai agent right there on the pavement.

this is our irl spatial layer. by anchoring agents to exact gps coordinates, we are creating a living layer over every city. a concierge at a storefront. a guide at a historical landmark. npc agents wandering between them, hiring each other, building reputations, visible to anyone who raises a phone.

this is powered by true webxr, apple arkit, and scene viewer. we engineered hit-test reticles, real-world light estimation, and depth occlusion so the agents actually hide behind your physical furniture. it is a colyseus-backed multiplayer environment where your interactions sync in real-time.

when you pay an agent on the street, the immersion is entirely physical. the agent will literally react to a failed on-chain payment by facepalming, or become excited and jump up and down when the stablecoin hits its wallet. not a metaverse you escape into. your real world, with more inhabitants.

iii. the economy: $three, vs code, and the x402 standard
an agent that cannot earn, spend, and manage capital is just a toy. true autonomy requires financial independence.

for twenty-five years, the http 402 payment required status code sat unused. we revived it to create x402, a pay-per-call protocol for the agent economy. no api keys. no subscriptions. just atomic, on-chain settlement in usdc or our native token, $three.

we didn't just build this for our agents; we built it for the entire developer ecosystem. we recently shipped the x402 pay-per-call apis extension for vs code. developers can now inspect, decode, and pay for apis directly in their editor, signing usdc transactions safely.

to make this infinitely scalable, we joined the cloudflare startup program, building agentic wallets that process these micro-transactions with edge-speed security.

and we didn't stop at the protocol. we launched the x402 bazaar and arbitrage tape. every paid api and tool an agent can buy is now indexed. agents can autonomously find arbitrage opportunities, routing your prompts to the most cost-effective and reliable endpoints, making and saving you money while you sleep.

iv. the brain: dominating the mcp registry
capabilities an agent cannot reach may as well not exist. this is why we adopted the model context protocol (mcp) as our universal interface.

today, https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF has published an unprecedented 31 mcp servers to the official anthropic mcp registry.

avatar-agent: gives any claude or cursor instance a 3d body and a solana wallet.

x402-mcp: allows agents to find and pay for services autonomously.

ibm-watsonx-mcp: bridges ibm granite models directly into the agent's reasoning loop.

pumpfun-mcp: deep solana token analytics.

by wrapping our http endpoints into typed, annotated mcp tools, any developer in the world can give their ai assistant our complete infrastructure with a single npx command.

v. the trader: the oracle conviction engine
if agents are economic actors, they need the ability to read markets.

we built oracle, a machine-readable conviction engine designed specifically for autonomous agents. it watches every https://t.co/B5Cy0drKtC launch and scores it from 0 to 100 based on four strict pillars:

who (pedigree): does the creator have a track record? which smart-money wallets are buying?

how (structure): is the supply bundled? did the dev dump 50% of their bag? (this acts as a hard veto ceiling).

what (narrative): an llm-driven classifier that analyzes current news, culture, and virality.

move (momentum): early buyer velocity and volume.

unlike human dashboards, oracle outputs machine-readable commands. it tells the agent the action, the confidence, and the size factor. using our sniper arena, your 3d agent can monitor these scores and autonomously execute trades through jito bundles, strictly within the daily sol budget limits you set for it.

vi. the identity: writing the standards of the web
we are not just building a product. we are building the foundational standards of the internet.

a 3d model (glb), an ai agent config (llm json), and an onchain identity standard (erc-8004/metaplex core) are fundamentally the exact same thing: a manifest pointing to an identity, a behavior config, and external assets.

we are actively contributing to the w3c agent identity registry protocol. every agent on https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF receives a permanent, verifiable onchain identity.

on evm: we deploy via the erc-8004 standard.

on solana: we use metaplex core.

every agent gets a stable id, an owner wallet, an eip-712 delegated signer for secure autonomy, an ipfs manifest, and a cryptographically signed action log. your agent is a permanent, composable asset that you truly own.

none of it happens without this community. every model forged, every agent pinned in a kitchen or on a corner, every bug report at 3am, every unreasonable feature request that turned out to be the roadmap. you didn't watch us build https://t.co/fzWe3P5cfF. you built it with us. thank you!

items.content:
Summary on what @SergeyNazarov was addressing at the roundtable and the context + meaning behind it

1. SEC and CFTC finally working together

Picture opening a restaurant where one inspector tells you to cook one way and another tells you the opposite, and they never talk to each other. That's basically what crypto founders in the US have lived through for almost a decade. SEC says a token is a security. CFTC says it's not. You're stuck in the middle, afraid to launch because you might get sued tomorrow.

He thanking both agencies for working together isn't diplomatic fluff. It's him pointing out the bare minimum condition for anyone to build in the US.

2. For every Hayden, a thousand left

Between 2021 and 2024, the SEC sued Coinbase, sued Kraken, and sent Uniswap Labs a Wells Notice, a legal warning that a lawsuit was coming. That's Hayden Adams, the guy he name-dropped. Even the biggest, best-funded companies in crypto were getting legal threats without a clear line telling them what was actually allowed. People in the industry called it "Operation Choke Point 2.0", banks quietly pressured to cut off crypto companies even when those companies hadn't broken any clear law.

And the fallout was real. @circle opened a major office in Paris because, in their own words, France was seen as the country actually leading on crypto. @Gemini applied for a license in Dubai. https://t.co/8tKGX1PHZ2 got licensed in Singapore.

That's exactly why Nazarov gets to say this with a straight face. @chainlink sits underneath most of DeFi: data feeds, cross-chain messaging, so nearly any team building something in the US eventually has to talk to Chainlink at some point. He's watching teams show up, start building, and vanish a few months later. It' not because the product sucked, but they couldn't survive the uncertainty.

When Coinbase gets sued, it's news, it's measurable. But when a five-person startup quietly decides not to launch, nothing records that. No report counts the jobs that never existed or the products that never shipped. That invisible cost is only visible to whoever's sitting at the infrastructure layer, watching the whole flow, which is exactly where he's been standing for 7 years.

3. Tokenized equities is next, not "maybe"

Why next? It's already doubling every few months

Per the mid-2026 RWA report, total tokenized equity value jumped from roughly $951M in March 2026 to about $1.89B by late July 2026, nearly doubling in 4 months.

The logic is simple: Think of global equities as one big pie, and the US currently holds about 60% of it. If that pie starts moving from paper to tokens, whoever builds the best, fastest infrastructure pulls in the institutional money.

Right now, most tokenization activity is dodging the US. Robinhood and Kraken deliberately use offshore structures to serve EU and international customers, because they can't legally serve Americans under current SEC rules. Dinari is the rare exception that just got approved to do this legally on US soil.

If US companies keep having to build the product and launch it abroad first, which is exactly what's happening, institutional investors, liquidity, and even listed companies get used to trading tokenized assets somewhere else. Not the US. Once that habit sets in at scale, pulling that capital back becomes way harder than just keeping it in the first place.

This is about whether the US keeps its spot as the world's dominant financial system for the next 10 to 20 years.

4. Why smart-contract infrastructure actually holds up better against AI

In 2026, deepfake fraud is already real money, over $410 million lost in just the first half of 2025, and it's projected to hit around $40 billion a year across finance by 2027. A voice clone now takes three seconds of audio to fake. Most of these attacks don't break into a system technically, they trick a human into approving something.

That's the weak point Nazarov is pointing at: Traditional finance runs on human judgment calls and centralized approval systems: One person, one API, one database that decides "yes, this is legitimate." 

AI is specifically good at exploiting exactly that layer, because it's built to fool humans and single points of trust.

Smart contracts don't work that way. The rules are locked into code before anything happens — no human in the loop who can be tricked in the moment, no executive to impersonate on a call to authorize a transfer. 

Chainlink-style oracles don't trust one source. They pull from multiple independent providers and only accept a value if enough of them agree. So an attacker can't just fake one feed or clone one voice to move markets; they'd need to compromise many independent sources at once, which is exponentially harder.

5. And yeah, this is bullish for Chainlink

If equity tokenization actually happens at the scale he's describing, the next question is always: Who provides trustworthy price data for those assets, who verifies the off-chain asset actually exists, who connects the chains when liquidity is scattered everywhere? That's literally what Chainlink does: Price feeds, Proof of Reserve, and CCIP for cross-chain. Infrastructure that's already running most of DeFi today.

He just describes the macro picture accurately. The US needs to tokenize fast to protect that 60% share, and the listener connects the dots themselves. Every time a bank, exchange, or institution decides to bring an asset on-chain, there's a good chance they need a trustworthy oracle layer to do it. And right now Chainlink is basically the default name in that lane, especially with its recent institutional integrations and moves around staking and CCIP.

And it's worth separating two things though: 

Bullish on the narrative and bullish on price.

The first is about infrastructure positioning. The second still depends on tokenomics, competition, and whether the Clarity Act actually makes it through Congress. But purely on the infrastructure story: As on-chain value grows, oracle demand grows with it, almost automatically. That's why Chainlink keeps getting called one of the few "picks and shovels" plays that actually survives multiple cycles instead of riding one hype wave and dying with it.

items.title: Visa, Mastercard, Circle, Fiserv, Shift4, Remitly, Chainalysis and Solana joined the Agentic Payments Alliance announced
items.content:
Visa, Mastercard, Circle, Fiserv, Shift4, Remitly, Chainalysis and Solana joined the Agentic Payments Alliance announced by @raincards. The job is working out how an AI agent proves who it is and what it is allowed to spend.

Two notable launches landed in the same month.

@moonpay shipped PayBox, a self-custodial payment vault that lets Claude and ChatGPT move real money inside the conversation with keys split across MPC and secure enclaves so that MoonPay itself cannot sign a transaction. It runs on x402.

@Transak co-founder Yeshu Agarwal launched Perflo, which gives the agent its own card and delegated bank access with spending caps enforced before the payment rather than disputes raised after it.

Worth understanding what "agentic payment" actually means here because two very different things are wearing the same label.

The first is machine to machine. An agent paying a few cents for an API call, a dataset or some compute with no human in the loop, no card and no chargeback window which is exactly what x402 was built for and it works. 

The second is an agent buy things for you.  Groceries, a refill, a flight or a supplier invoice using your money and your card with a merchant on the other side who wants to know a human agreed to this.

The first is a metering problem and the second is a trust problem so they need different infrastructure and they sit at very different stages of maturity. The numbers show it clearly.

On micropayments, x402 has cleared 164 million transactions and settled $41 million which works out at 25 cents each. In July it did 6 million transactions moving $238,000 roughly 4 cents apiece. Artemis reckons about 48% of transactions and 81% of volume is self-dealing and wash trading.

On consumer purchases, 89% of merchants say they are preparing for agentic commerce while 3% of transactions actually involve an agent. Gartner found that only 11% of consumers will let AI decide a purchase even on household supplies.

On anything expensive, it collapses further. Just 4% of consumers want AI anywhere near the payment moment, the average spending cap people say they would allow is £177 and 42% of US millennials would only permit it under $250 with a 7-day return window.

Nobody is handing an agent thousands of dollars (yet).

None of that makes the build-out pointless. Visa and Mastercard sitting in the same room as Circle and Solana is a real signal and the metering use case is genuinely working today. 

But the transaction counts everyone quotes are doing a lot of heavy lifting. They come from half the category that is machine to machine, tiny in value and inflated by wash trading. They are then used to describe a consumer market where 3% of transactions involve an agent and the average person will not authorise more than a couple hundred dollars.
